title: Introduction to Cybersecurity
summary: What cybersecurity is, why it matters to everyone, and the simple habits that block most attacks.
intro: Cybersecurity means protecting your phone, computer, accounts and information from people who want to steal, damage or misuse them. You don’t need to be technical. Most attacks succeed because someone was rushed or tricked, not because a hacker out-smarted a computer.
objectives: Explain what cybersecurity is in plain words
Name the most common threats ordinary people face
Apply five basic habits that reduce your risk

p: Our lives now run through phones: banking, school, work, chats and shopping. That makes your accounts valuable to criminals, whether you are a student, a trader or a company manager.
Attackers often choose easy targets over rich ones. Good basic habits make you a harder target.

Security experts talk about three goals: confidentiality (only the right people see your information), integrity (it isn’t changed without permission) and availability (you can use it when you need it).
Losing access to your WhatsApp account, having your savings drained, or having a stranger read your messages are each a failure of one of these goals.

example.title: Example: a rushed tap
example.text: Ada receives an SMS saying her account will be blocked. She taps the link and enters her details on a page that looks right. Within minutes her account is emptied. The page was fake, and the only thing that would have stopped it was pausing to check.

prevention: Use a different strong password for every important account
Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA)
Install updates for your phone and apps
Only install apps from official stores
Pause before you click, pay or share a code
takeaways: Everyone is a possible target
Most attacks trick people, not computers
Small habits stop most attacks

title: Password Security
summary: Build strong, unique passwords, use a password manager and turn on two-factor authentication.
intro: A password is the key to your digital life. Weak or reused passwords are one of the easiest ways for criminals to get in. The good news: strong passwords are simple to create once you know how.
objectives: Create long, hard-to-guess passphrases
Understand why you must never reuse passwords
Set up 2FA on your most important accounts

p: Length beats complexity. A passphrase made of several unrelated words (for example, four random words and a number) is both strong and easier to remember than a short jumble of symbols.
Avoid names, birthdays, phone numbers and common words such as “password” or “123456”. Attackers try these first.
When a website is breached, criminals try the leaked passwords on other sites. If you reuse a password, one leak can open many accounts.
A password manager creates and stores a different strong password for each account, so you only remember one master passphrase.
2FA asks for a second proof, such as a code from an authenticator app, after your password. Even if someone steals your password, they still can’t get in.
Never share a one-time code with anyone. Genuine support teams do not ask for it.

example.title: Example: weak vs strong
example.text: Weak: password123 or your date of birth. Stronger: a passphrase like river-lantern-maize-torch-47, kept in a password manager and protected with 2FA.

prevention: Use at least 12 characters, longer for email and banking
Never reuse passwords across accounts
Use a reputable password manager
Enable 2FA, preferring an authenticator app or security key over SMS
Change a password immediately if you suspect a leak
takeaways: Long and unique beats short and complex
One leak shouldn’t open all your accounts
2FA is your safety net. Never share the codes

title: Phishing and Email Security
summary: Recognise fake emails, SMS and links, and know exactly what to do if you clicked.
intro: Phishing is when criminals pretend to be a bank, a company or someone you know to trick you into revealing information or clicking something harmful. It arrives by email, SMS (smishing), phone calls (vishing) and social media messages.
objectives: Spot the common signs of phishing
Check links and sender addresses safely
Respond correctly if you clicked or shared details

p: Urgency or threats (“your account will be blocked”), requests for passwords, PINs, BVN or OTPs, shortened or odd-looking links, generic greetings, and sender addresses that almost match the real company.
Messages can look perfect. Don’t rely on spelling mistakes alone, because modern scams are often well written.
Don’t use the link in the message. Open the official app or type the website address yourself.
Check the full sender address, not just the display name. On a computer, hover over links to preview where they go. On a phone, press and hold.
Don’t panic. Change the password for that account straight away (and anywhere you reused it), turn on 2FA, check recent activity and tell your bank if money or card details were involved.

example.title: Example: fake bank SMS
example.text: “ALERT: ₦150,000 debit on your account. Not you? Your account will be blocked in 30 minutes. Confirm your BVN and OTP at bit.ly/secure-acct.” This message uses fear, a deadline, a hidden link and a request for secrets, so it has four red flags.

prevention: Never share OTPs, PINs or passwords by message or call
Open the official app or type the address yourself
Treat urgent messages with extra suspicion
Report phishing to your bank or email provider
Keep 2FA on your email account, since it unlocks everything else
takeaways: Urgency + a link + a request for secrets is a red flag
Go to the official app, don’t use the link
If you clicked, change passwords and tell your bank

title: Social Engineering
summary: How attackers manipulate trust, fear and urgency, and how to keep your head.
intro: Social engineering is the art of manipulating people rather than computers. Attackers pretend to be someone you trust and use emotions such as fear, greed, kindness or urgency to make you act without thinking.
objectives: Recognise common manipulation tactics
Understand pretexting, baiting and tailgating
Use a simple verify-first habit

p: Pretexting: inventing a believable story, such as a caller claiming to be from your telecom company. Baiting: leaving a tempting item, like a free USB drive. Tailgating: following someone through a secured door.
Impersonation of bosses, relatives or officials is especially common because we want to be helpful.
Real organisations allow you time to check. Pressure to act now, keep it secret, or skip normal steps is the biggest sign something is wrong.

example.title: Example: the “boss” on WhatsApp
example.text: A message from your manager’s picture asks you to buy airtime vouchers urgently and send the codes. The number is new. Calling your manager on their known number shows it’s fake.

prevention: Verify requests through a second channel you already trust
Be wary of urgency, secrecy and unusual payment methods
Don’t plug in unknown USB drives
Challenge unknown visitors politely
Share less personal information publicly
takeaways: Attackers target emotions, not machines
Pressure and secrecy are warning signs
Verify through a separate trusted channel

title: Online Scams and Fraud Prevention
summary: Spot fake investments, advance-fee tricks, fake shops, loan apps and romance scams.
intro: Online scams cost people money, trust and peace of mind. Scammers adapt quickly, but most schemes follow the same patterns: a promise that is too good, a reason to hurry and a request for money or information.
objectives: Recognise the patterns behind common scams
Check a seller, offer or investor before paying
Know what to do if you’ve been scammed

p: Fake investments promising guaranteed high returns; advance-fee scams (“pay a fee to receive a prize or job”); fake online shops; overpayment tricks; romance or impersonation scams; and predatory loan apps that misuse your contacts and photos.

Search for independent reviews, check the real business address and phone number, prefer payment methods that offer protection (such as pay-on-delivery), and be suspicious of anyone who pushes you off the platform or asks for gift cards or transfers to personal accounts.
Ask a trusted friend. Scammers hate second opinions.

Stop contact, tell your bank at once, keep screenshots and receipts, report to the platform and the relevant authorities, and warn friends. Being scammed is not shameful. It happens to careful people.

example.title: Example: the job fee
example.text: An advert for a “guaranteed” office job asks for a ₦10,000 registration fee. After payment, the contact disappears. Real employers do not charge you to hire you.

prevention: If it sounds too good to be true, it is
Never pay to receive a prize, loan, job or scholarship
Use regulated lenders and platforms
Check names and numbers before every transfer
Talk to someone before you pay
takeaways: Urgency + a promise of easy money is a warning
Never pay a fee to receive something
Report quickly. Speed can save your money

title: Mobile Device Security
summary: Protect your phone with locks, updates, safe apps and sensible permissions.
intro: For many people, the phone is the main computer. It holds your messages, photos, banking apps and identity. A few settings make it much safer.
objectives: Secure a phone with a strong lock and find-my-device
Choose apps and permissions carefully
Understand SIM swap fraud

p: Use a strong PIN, password or biometric lock (avoid 1234 or 0000). Turn on find-my-device so you can locate, lock or erase a lost phone. Install system and app updates promptly because they fix security flaws.
Install apps only from your official app store. Free “modded” or cracked apps from links are a common source of malware. Check permissions: a flashlight does not need your contacts.

In a SIM swap, a criminal convinces your network provider to move your number to their SIM, then receives your calls and OTP codes. Warning sign: your phone suddenly loses all signal. Contact your provider and bank immediately.

example.title: Example: odd permissions
example.text: A photo-editing app asks to read your contacts and SMS. Neither is needed to edit photos, so deny them, or choose another app.

prevention: Use a strong screen lock and find-my-device
Update the system and apps
Install from official stores only
Review app permissions regularly
Protect your SIM with a PIN and watch for sudden loss of signal
takeaways: Your phone is a vault. Lock it
Fewer permissions means less risk
Sudden loss of signal can be a SIM swap warning

title: Internet and Browser Safety
summary: Browse safely: check addresses, avoid risky downloads and understand what HTTPS really means.
intro: The web is full of useful things, and some traps. Safe browsing is mostly about checking where you are and being careful about what you download.
objectives: Read web addresses correctly
Understand what the padlock and HTTPS do and don’t mean
Avoid unsafe downloads and pop-ups

p: The part just before the first single slash is the real site. In “bank.example.com.secure-login.net”, the real site is secure-login.net. Look-alike spellings (“paypa1”) are used to trick you.
HTTPS means the connection is encrypted. It doesn’t guarantee the site is honest, because scam sites can use HTTPS too.
Download software only from official sources. Be sceptical of pop-ups saying your device is infected, or telling you to update your browser. Close them and go to your settings yourself.

example.title: Example: fake update
example.text: A banner says “Your browser is out of date. Click to update.” The file is malware. Real browsers update themselves through settings.

prevention: Check the address before entering any password
Keep the browser updated
Use official download sites
Don’t click pop-up alerts, close the tab
Consider a reputable ad blocker and browser safe-browsing protection
takeaways: The real site is the part before the first single slash
HTTPS = encrypted, not necessarily honest
Pop-ups that scare you are usually scams

title: Social Media Security
summary: Lock down your accounts, share less and avoid hijacking on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and more.
intro: Social media makes it easy to connect, and easy for criminals to study you, copy your identity or take over your account to scam your friends.
objectives: Secure social and messaging accounts
Decide what is safe to post
Recognise account hijacking and fake profiles

p: Use a unique password and 2FA on every social and messaging account. On WhatsApp, turn on two-step verification and never share the 6-digit registration code.
Don’t post boarding passes, ID cards, tickets, your full birth date, home address or real-time location. Use privacy settings to limit who sees your posts and contacts.
Fake profiles and cloned accounts are common. Check mutual contacts and be cautious with strangers and sudden money requests from “friends”.

example.title: Example: the hijacked friend
example.text: A friend’s account messages you: “Please help, I’m stranded, send ₦20,000.” Their account was taken over. Call them to check before you send anything.

prevention: Unique password + 2FA on every account
Turn on WhatsApp two-step verification
Review privacy settings every few months
Never share verification codes
Report and block impersonators
takeaways: Your account can be used to scam your friends
Share less, secure more
Never share verification codes

title: Data Privacy and Protection
summary: Understand your personal data, your rights and how to share the minimum needed.
intro: Your personal data, such as your name, phone number, BVN, NIN, photos and location, has value. Privacy means having a say in who collects it, why and what they do with it.
objectives: Identify what counts as personal data
Share only what is necessary
Know that data protection laws give you rights

p: Identifiers (BVN, NIN, passport and ID numbers), contact details, financial information, health information, location and photos. The more of these a criminal holds, the easier it is to impersonate you.
Before giving data, ask: does this organisation really need it, and how will it be used? Check privacy settings in apps, and review permissions regularly.

In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for organisations that handle personal data and gives individuals rights over it. Read the official guidance from the Nigeria Data Protection Commission for details.

example.title: Example: the competition form
example.text: A competition asks for your NIN “to verify you”. A genuine competition rarely needs it. Ask why, and decline if the reason isn’t clear.

prevention: Share only the data that is necessary
Mark ID copies with their purpose and date
Review app permissions and privacy settings
Use messaging apps with end-to-end encryption
Shred papers with personal details
takeaways: Your data has value. Share it deliberately
Ask why it’s needed and how it will be used
The law gives you rights. Learn them

title: Ransomware and Malware
summary: What malicious software is, how it spreads and how backups beat ransomware.
intro: Malware is software designed to harm or spy on you. It includes viruses, spyware, adware and ransomware, which locks your files until you pay.
objectives: Name the main types of malware
Know how malware commonly spreads
Prepare backups and respond to an infection

p: Viruses and worms spread between devices. Spyware and keyloggers watch what you do. Adware floods you with ads. Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment. Trojans pretend to be useful software.

Unexpected attachments, cracked software, fake updates, malicious ads, infected USB drives and links in messages. Keeping software updated and downloading only from official sources prevents most infections.

Keep at least one backup separate from your main device (an external drive kept disconnected, or a cloud service with version history) and test that you can restore it. If you are infected, disconnect from the network and seek help rather than paying.

example.title: Example: the free download
example.text: A cracked copy of paid software installs a hidden program that records keystrokes. The “saving” costs the victim’s bank login.

prevention: Update the system, apps and browser
Download only from official sources
Don’t open unexpected attachments
Use reputable security software
Keep tested offline or cloud backups
takeaways: Most malware arrives through tricks, not magic
Backups are the best answer to ransomware
If infected, disconnect and get help

title: Network Security
summary: Secure your router, understand firewalls and use VPNs sensibly.
intro: A network connects your devices to each other and to the internet. If the network is weak, everything on it is exposed.
objectives: Secure a home or small-office router
Explain what firewalls and VPNs do
Segment guests from your main devices

p: Change the default admin password and the Wi-Fi password, keep the router’s firmware updated, and disable features you don’t use. Default logins like admin/admin are public knowledge.

A firewall filters traffic, blocking connections you didn’t ask for. A VPN encrypts your traffic between your device and the VPN provider, which helps on untrusted networks. It is not a magic shield, and you should choose reputable providers.

example.title: Example: default password
example.text: A shop keeps the router’s factory login. Anyone nearby who guesses it can change settings or watch the traffic.

prevention: Change default router logins
Update router firmware
Use WPA3 or WPA2 with a long passphrase
Create a separate guest network
Turn off remote administration if unused
takeaways: Defaults are public knowledge. Change them
Firewalls block, VPNs encrypt
Separate guests from your main devices

title: Wi-Fi Security
summary: Stay safe on public and home Wi-Fi, and avoid fake hotspots.
intro: Wi-Fi is convenient, but you rarely know who runs a public network or who is watching it.
objectives: Recognise risks of public Wi-Fi
Spot fake hotspots
Set up secure home Wi-Fi

p: Criminals can set up look-alike networks (“evil twins”) with names like “Airport_Free_WiFi”. Ask staff for the exact network name. Avoid banking on public Wi-Fi, use mobile data when possible and use a VPN if you must connect.
Use WPA3 (or WPA2) with a long passphrase, change the default router name and password and check connected devices occasionally.

example.title: Example: the two airport networks
example.text: Two networks have almost the same name. One is a fake that captures everything typed. Confirm the exact name with staff.

prevention: Confirm the real network name
Prefer mobile data for banking
Use a VPN on untrusted networks
Turn off automatic Wi-Fi joining
Use WPA3/WPA2 at home
takeaways: Not every “Free WiFi” is real
Use mobile data for sensitive tasks
Strong passphrase at home

title: Identity Theft Prevention
summary: Protect IDs and personal data, spot early warning signs and act quickly.
intro: Identity theft happens when someone uses your personal details to open accounts, take loans or commit fraud in your name.
objectives: Know what details criminals want
Spot early warning signs
Respond quickly if your identity is misused

p: Names, dates of birth, ID and BVN or NIN numbers, addresses, card and bank details. They may get them from phishing, data breaches, discarded papers or over-sharing online.

Transactions or accounts you don’t recognise, unexpected bills, messages about accounts you didn’t open. Report to the institution and authorities at once, secure your email and passwords, and keep a record of every report.

example.title: Example: the ID photocopy
example.text: A copy of an ID card left at a business centre is reused to open an account. Writing “For X purpose, date” across copies makes misuse harder.

prevention: Shred documents with personal details
Mark ID copies with their purpose
Review statements and alerts
Use unique passwords and 2FA
Be careful what you post publicly
takeaways: Your ID details are valuable
Check statements and alerts regularly
Act quickly and keep records

title: Cybersecurity for Students
summary: Safe habits for school portals, shared computers, social media and online learning.
intro: Students are heavy internet users and frequent targets, from fake scholarships to account takeovers. Your online habits now can protect your future.
objectives: Secure portals, email and shared computers
Spot scholarship and job scams
Build a safe digital reputation

p: Your school email is the key to many things. Use a unique password and 2FA, never share portal logins and always sign out on shared computers.
Fake scholarships, internship fees, exam-leak offers and fake “free data” links. Legitimate scholarships don’t charge applicants to be selected. Check directly with the awarding organisation.

example.title: Example: the scholarship fee
example.text: A message says you were selected for a scholarship if you pay a “processing fee”. The real organisation’s website lists no such programme.

prevention: Unique password and 2FA for school email
Never share portal logins
Sign out of shared computers
Verify scholarship offers directly
Think before posting. Employers look
takeaways: Your school email is a master key
Real scholarships don’t charge applicants
Sign out on shared devices

title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses
summary: Simple, low-cost steps for SMEs to protect accounts, payments, customers and data.
intro: Small businesses are attractive targets because they hold money and customer data but often have few protections. The good news: basic steps prevent most common attacks.
objectives: Apply a basic security checklist
Prevent payment-change fraud
Plan backups and staff access

p: Unique passwords and 2FA for email, banking and social pages; updates on all devices; regular tested backups; antivirus on computers; and a list of who has access to what.
Criminals send a convincing email claiming a supplier’s bank details changed. Always confirm changes by phoning a known number before paying.
Remove access immediately when staff leave, and give people only the access they need.

example.title: Example: the changed account number
example.text: A buyer gets an email from the “supplier” with a new account number. They pay, and the real supplier never receives the money. A quick call would have prevented it.

prevention: 2FA on email, banking and social pages
Verify payment changes by phone
Regular, tested backups
Least-privilege access and prompt offboarding
Train staff to recognise phishing
takeaways: Basics prevent most attacks
Verify bank-detail changes by phone
Backups and access control protect the business

title: Cybersecurity Awareness for Organisations
summary: Build a security culture: training, reporting, access rules and incident planning.
intro: Technology alone can’t protect an organisation. People make daily decisions that attackers try to influence. A strong security culture turns staff into a defence.
objectives: Plan an awareness programme
Create a blame-free reporting culture
Prepare a basic incident response plan

p: Short, regular sessions beat one long annual lecture. Use real examples from your sector, simulated phishing exercises that teach rather than punish and clear guidance on what to do.
Write down who to call, how to isolate a device, how to preserve evidence and how to communicate. Practise it. Make reporting easy and blame-free so problems surface early.

example.title: Example: the quick report
example.text: An employee reports a suspicious email within minutes. IT blocks the sender before others click. The culture, not the technology, made the difference.

prevention: Regular short awareness sessions
Easy, blame-free reporting
Least-privilege access
A written, practised incident plan
Rules for personal devices used for work
takeaways: People are part of the defence
Make reporting easy and safe
Practise your incident plan

title: Safe Digital Payments
summary: Protect your cards, transfers, mobile money and POS or ATM use.
intro: Digital payments are fast, and so are mistakes and fraud. A few habits keep your money safer.
objectives: Protect PINs, OTPs and cards
Verify before you send a transfer
React quickly to suspicious alerts

p: Your PIN, OTP, CVV and password are for you alone. No bank, shop or agent needs them from you. Shield the keypad at ATMs and POS terminals and don’t accept help from strangers.
Check the beneficiary name and account number, be wary of requests to pay by gift cards or into personal accounts for “deposits”, and use virtual or low-balance cards for online shopping.
If you see a debit you didn’t make, contact your bank through its official app or number immediately and block the card.

example.title: Example: the clipboard swap
example.text: Some malware changes the account number you copied. Always re-read the account name and number before you confirm.

prevention: Never share PIN, OTP or CVV
Shield the keypad
Confirm beneficiary name and number
Use virtual or low-balance cards online
Act on suspicious alerts immediately
takeaways: PIN, OTP and CVV are never to be shared
Verify the account before sending
Report suspicious debits immediately

title: Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity
summary: How AI helps criminals and defenders, deepfakes, voice cloning and using AI tools safely.
intro: AI tools can write, speak and create images that look real. That helps both defenders and criminals. Knowing the risks lets you enjoy the benefits safely.
objectives: Understand how criminals use AI
Recognise deepfakes and voice-clone scams
Use AI tools without leaking private data

p: AI can write convincing phishing messages, clone a voice from a short clip and generate fake images or videos (deepfakes). The goal is the same: to make you trust, pay or share.

Don’t paste passwords, ID numbers or confidential business data into AI tools. Verify important facts, since AI can be confidently wrong. If a voice note or video asks for urgent money, verify with the person on a number you already have.

example.title: Example: the cloned voice
example.text: A voice note that sounds like your brother asks for urgent money. Calling him back on his known number reveals he sent nothing.

prevention: Verify urgent requests through a second channel
Don’t share secrets with AI tools
Check important facts from trusted sources
Be sceptical of too-perfect videos or audio
Agree a family safe word for emergencies
takeaways: AI makes scams more convincing
Verify urgent voice and video requests
Don’t put secrets into AI tools
